After a solid 2-year Treasury auction Monday, which saw an improvement in indirect demand, today’s $70 billion 5-year auction was back to the pattern of the auctions earlier this month, with weak indirect demand (which includes foreign buyers), in this case dropping to the least since March 2020.

Still, record direct demand helped lift overall demand to the best since August, but the auction nevertheless ended in the 13th straight tail (yield above expectations), which ZeroHedge calls the longest such stretch on record.

The details:

▪️ Indirect: 54.3%, lowest since March 2020, vs. 60.0% in October and a 61.9% six-month average.

▪️ Direct: 36.7%, a record since bidder data began in 2008, vs. 29.4% in October and a 25.5% six-month average (prior high: 31.7%, December 2025).

▪️ Dealers: 9.0%, lowest since December 2025, vs. 10.6% in October and a 12.6% six-month average.

▪️ Bid-to-cover: 2.37, highest since August, vs. 2.33 in October and a 2.31 six-month average.

▪️ Tail: +0.3 basis point (4.719% high yield vs. 4.716% when-issued), vs. +0.4 in October and a +0.9 six-month average.

▪️ High yield: 4.719%, lowest since August, vs. 4.845% in October and a 4.510% six-month average.

ZeroHedge called it “a very ugly 5Y auction,” saying “the internals were a mess.” That seems a little dramatic, as there’s nothing surprising about this auction tailing (it's the 13th in a row), and the shift from indirect to direct demand may reflect a change in how buyers are categorized more than anything. Still, it was the 10th straight note or bond auction with the indirect share below its six-month average.

Wednesday’s 7-year will wrap up the month.

BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky has been on a roll. He turned bearish on October 6, the day of the S&P 500's record close, and told clients on November 12 to sell the bounce near 7,600. The index then fell 9%. Friday morning he said a short-term bottom should come around 7,000. The S&P closed at 6,910 that day, then jumped 4.7% Monday to 7,237, its biggest one-day gain since April 2025.

Sunday he called for a short rally, then another leg lower:

▪️ The break below 7,000 and "a host of capitulatory signals" made this "at least a pitch we are willing to swing at," even without a "full-fledged breadth washout."
▪️ He doesn't think Friday was the final low. He's "looking for a short-term rally back towards 7250-7350 before likely turning lower again."

His case for another leg down hasn't changed - we haven't gotten enough of a washout. About half of S&P stocks were still above their 50-day moving averages last week, vs. a median of 11% at lows after 8%+ pullbacks since 1997. And Apple is only about 3% off its high, vs. a median of 23% at S&P bottoms since 2015.

One caveat: since 2024 he has often leaned too bearish. By my count he was right on 9 of 21 S&P calls since mid-2024. But most of the misses came from staying bearish too long, after lows were in or during the 2024–25 rally. But he called for downside ahead of or during each of the last four pullbacks, and he's 5 for his last 8.

Monday's close is already within about 0.2% of the low end of his target, and the top of the zone lines up with the 200-day moving average near 7,348. If his roadmap holds, that's where to reduce risk. A break above that might signal he held a bearish view too long again.

The Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumped 11.4 points in November to 103.3, the highest since January 2025, topping every estimate in Bloomberg's survey. The 11.4-point rise was the biggest since May 2025, per ZeroHedge, and a second straight beat of more than 10 points.

▪ Present Situation: 132.8 (+13.7), the highest since July 2025, per Bloomberg.
▪ Expectations: 83.6 (+9.9), the best since the end of 2024 per Bloomberg, and back above 80 for the first time this year.
▪ Four of five components improved; only expected income eased.
▪ Jobs "plentiful": 30.8%, the highest of 2026. "Hard to get": 18.4%, the lowest of 2026. The gap (+12.4) is the widest of the year and more than four times July's low.
▪ Expected jobs: net −1.2%, from −10.4%, the least pessimistic reading of the year.
▪ Expected business conditions turned positive (+2.3%) for the first time this year.
▪ Average 12-month inflation expectations: 5.7%, down for a second month.

One of the charts in last night's @DailyChartbook nightly email was from Carson's great @RyanDetrick, noting that "faster 10% corrections historically haven't been as likely to fall into a bear market." Since 1928, those that hit −10% within 20 trading days of a record became bear markets 3 of 9 times, vs. 9 of 17 slower ones.

I dug into the data, and fast corrections haven't just been less likely to turn into bears. They've also tended to bounce back faster.

This one took 33 trading days to reach −10% (October 6 record to Friday's close). Looking at corrections that got there in 33 days or fewer since 1928:

▪️ 4 of 11 (36%) became bear markets, vs. 8 of 15 (53%) for slower ones.
▪️ The bottom came a median of just 17 trading days after the first −10% close, vs. 112 for slower corrections.
▪️ The S&P's median return from that first −10% close was +16.8% over the next 6 months (9 of 11 higher), vs. +3.0% for slower corrections and +4.9% for all days since 1928.
▪️ 12 months out, the median gain was +17.6% (8 of 11 higher), vs. +7.0%.
▪️ They got back to a new record in a median of 126 trading days, vs. 375 for slower corrections.

The exceptions were 1929 and 2007, two not great years, so it's not a guarantee. But history says the speed of this pullback is more a feature than a bug, and Monday's +4.7% rally is a decent start.

So while Fed members have been insistent on a broadening of price pressures, according to this study at least, the past year's acceleration in core PCE came from fuel.

The usual caveats apply. The authors say these estimates are imprecise and assume historical relationships still hold. The VAR model also leaves core without the fuel effect near 3%, still well above the Fed's 2% target, so on that estimate underlying inflation is still too high even if it isn't accelerating.

Still, the direction is the same on every model, and the fuel boost is set to reverse just as the Fed may be completing an accelerated hiking cycle.
